strengths: The core idea is simple, well-motivated, and technically plausible: horizontally concatenating KV caches from adjacent layers and sharing the left singular basis is a natural way to exploit cross-layer redundancy, and the CKA/eigenvalue analysis gives useful evidence that token-wise cosine similarity misses this structure.

The empirical results are fairly broad for a KV-cache compression paper: the paper evaluates Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5 7B/14B long-context models, and DeepSeek-Coder-V2 with MLA, covering both standard long-context RULER tasks and coding benchmarks.

The main accuracy/compression tradeoff is convincing within the tested setting. xKV substantially outperforms Single SVD at high compression and MiniCache at even modest compression, while remaining nearly lossless around 2.2-2.5x compression on several models.

The method is post-training and architecture-light for standard attention models, which makes the contribution practically attractive compared with methods that require retraining or architectural redesign.
The paper includes useful ablations separating key and value compression and acknowledges important limitations around fixed rank allocation and missing end-to-end system integration.
weaknesses: The practical systems claim is under-supported. The paper reports nominal KV-cache compression and accuracy, but does not measure actual peak memory, decoding latency, throughput, GPU utilization, or reconstruction overhead in a real inference engine. Since xKV requires reconstructing layer-specific K/V states during decoding, the true deployment tradeoff is central and remains unresolved.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The abstract says code is publicly available, but the manuscript text shows an empty code link. Important details such as exact rank choices, rank-to-compression accounting, hardware, SVD implementation, batching, context lengths beyond 64k, and wall-clock overhead are either missing or only briefly described.

The comparison set is narrow. MiniCache and Single SVD are relevant, but the paper does not compare against strong practical KV-cache compression systems such as quantization, eviction/sparse attention methods, or hybrid low-rank methods like ShadowKV-style deployments. This weakens claims about addressing long-context memory bottlenecks broadly.

The reported headline comparison to MiniCache is somewhat fragile because MiniCache achieves only 1.2-1.3x compression in the authors' setup and was reimplemented by the authors due to unavailable code. Without stronger validation of that reimplementation, the “6.8x higher compression” claim may overstate the evidence.

The method’s computational cost is not analyzed rigorously. Online SVD over long prompts may be expensive, and the claim that overhead is less than 10% at 128k is not supported by tables, hardware details, or scaling curves. The paper also does not clarify whether reconstruction is materialized per layer or fused into attention.

The theoretical motivation around CKA is helpful but limited. High CKA suggests overlap of dominant left singular subspaces, but the appendix does not give actionable error bounds for cross-layer SVD compression or connect CKA values quantitatively to downstream accuracy preservation.

Evaluation is mostly at a single 64k context length for RULER, despite motivating very long contexts up to 1M tokens. The paper would be stronger with scaling results over context length and with tests on more natural long-context workloads, including long generation where uncompressed newly generated KV states may no longer be negligible.

Presentation has several rough edges, including grammar issues, inconsistent method naming, a missing code URL, and some unclear terminology around “compression rate” versus rank ratio. These do not invalidate the work, but they reduce confidence in the polish and reproducibility of the submission.

strengths: The paper identifies a plausible and useful source of redundancy in KV caches: adjacent layers can have poorly aligned token-wise vectors but more aligned dominant singular/token subspaces. The CKA and eigenvalue analyses give a reasonable motivation for cross-layer low-rank compression.

The proposed method is simple and post-training: concatenate KV caches from grouped adjacent layers, compute a shared low-rank factor, and keep layer-specific reconstruction matrices. This makes the idea easy to understand and potentially easy to integrate with existing inference code.

The main RULER results show meaningful accuracy/compression tradeoffs relative to the authors' single-layer SVD baseline and their MiniCache reimplementation. At moderate compression, xKV is close to lossless, and at high compression it is much more robust than single-layer SVD in the reported settings.

The paper includes several models, including Llama-3.1, Qwen2.5 long-context models, and an MLA-based DeepSeek-Coder variant, which helps demonstrate that the idea is not tied to only one architecture.
The limitations section honestly notes missing end-to-end serving evaluation and the possible cost of reconstruction FLOPs. This is a useful disclosure rather than a weakness by itself.
weaknesses: The central practical claim is under-supported because there is no complete system evaluation of latency, throughput, memory bandwidth, prefill cost, decode speed, batching, or concurrency. KV-cache compression is primarily a serving-systems problem, and reporting benchmark accuracy plus nominal compression ratios is not enough to establish that xKV improves real long-context inference.

The method requires on-the-fly SVD over long-context KV tensors during prefill, but the evidence for overhead is very thin: the paper states it is under 10% of prefill time at 128k without giving hardware, batch size, implementation details, rank settings, variance across models, or scaling behavior. This is a major soundness gap for a method whose practicality depends on this cost.

The comparison set is too narrow. The paper mainly compares against MiniCache and per-layer SVD, while many relevant KV-cache methods are cited but not experimentally compared, including quantization, token eviction, ShadowKV-like systems, and recent low-rank/progressive compression approaches. The claim of state-of-the-art inter-layer compression is therefore only partially substantiated, and the broader usefulness relative to practical alternatives is unclear.

The MiniCache comparison is fragile because the authors reimplement it due to unavailable code. The paper does not provide enough validation that the reimplementation matches the original method, yet several headline claims rely on MiniCache performing very poorly at only 1.2-1.3x compression.

Reproducibility is weak. The abstract says code is publicly available but the extracted manuscript shows a blank link, and the paper omits important details such as exact ranks for each compression point, SVD algorithm, precision, hardware, batching, random seeds, and full evaluation protocol. This makes the reported tradeoffs hard to verify.

The evaluation is limited mostly to RULER at 64k and two code-completion datasets for the MLA case. There is no evaluation across context lengths, generation lengths, multi-turn or very long-output settings, real retrieval/code workloads, or robustness to different prompt distributions, despite the method being motivated by long-context deployment.

The theoretical/diagnostic argument is suggestive but not very deep. High CKA implies weighted overlap of left singular subspaces, but the paper does not show when this translates into low attention error, output distribution preservation, or stable decoding after repeated reconstruction across layers. The bridge from subspace alignment to model quality is mostly empirical.

Compression accounting is not fully transparent. It is unclear whether reported rates include all stored factors, uncompressed generated-token cache, RoPE keys for MLA, temporary memory during SVD, and reconstruction buffers. These details matter for real memory savings.

Presentation is generally readable, but there are several rough edges: grammatical errors, an empty code URL, inconsistent capitalization/notation, and claims such as 'significantly' or 'state-of-the-art' that are stronger than the evidence supports.

Research ethics risks appear limited because this is an inference-efficiency method, but the paper does not meaningfully discuss downstream misuse implications of cheaper long-context serving or environmental tradeoffs from added computation versus memory savings. This is not a decisive flaw, but the broader impacts section is minimal.

strengths: The paper identifies a useful and plausible source of redundancy in KV caches: although adjacent-layer token embeddings may have low cosine similarity, their dominant left singular-vector subspaces can be well aligned as measured by CKA. This gives a coherent motivation for cross-layer SVD rather than simple layer merging.

The proposed method is simple, post-training, and architecture-preserving: concatenate KV caches from a group of layers, compute a shared low-rank token basis, and keep layer-specific reconstruction matrices. This is an appealing contribution because it can apply to existing models without retraining.

The empirical results are strong on the central benchmark. On RULER at 64k context, xKV consistently outperforms both MiniCache and per-layer SVD, especially at high compression; e.g., Llama-3.1-8B retains 87.8 average accuracy at about 8x compression with xKV-4 versus 35.3 for single-layer SVD, and Qwen2.5 models show similar trends.

The paper usefully tests more than one model family and includes an MLA-based DeepSeek-Coder-V2 setting, showing that the idea is not limited to standard GQA caches. The key/value ablation also helps explain where compression is more or less robust.
The limitations section is honest about important deployment gaps, especially the absence of an end-to-end serving-system evaluation and the use of fixed rank allocation.
weaknesses: The main missing evidence is systems-level validation. Since the method requires online SVD during prefill and reconstruction during decode, memory compression alone does not establish practical throughput or latency gains. The paper reports less than 10% prefill overhead at 128k but does not provide detailed wall-clock, throughput, batching, GPU-memory, or decode-speed measurements.

The comparison set is somewhat narrow. The paper compares primarily against MiniCache and single-layer online SVD, but omits or does not deeply compare to several strong practical KV-compression families such as quantization, token eviction/sparse KV methods, and recent low-rank projection approaches under matched memory budgets.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the manuscript as written. It says the code is publicly available, but the URL appears blank in the abstract, and important implementation details such as exact ranks per compression point, SVD implementation choices, hardware, latency measurement setup, and benchmark decoding settings are not fully specified.

The theoretical/analytical support is suggestive rather than definitive. The CKA derivation connects high CKA to weighted singular-vector overlap, but it does not by itself establish when cross-layer SVD will preserve downstream attention behavior or how approximation errors propagate across layers.

The evaluation is concentrated on 64k RULER plus two code-completion datasets for the MLA case. Given the long-context motivation, results across longer contexts, more natural generation workloads, and very long-output scenarios would better support the broad deployment claims.

Presentation is generally clear, but there are several polish issues: some grammar errors, a missing code link, occasional overclaiming around compression-rate superiority, and limited detail in figures/tables about how compression ratios map to ranks and storage accounting.

strengths: The paper identifies a useful structural property of KV caches: despite low token-wise cosine similarity across adjacent layers, CKA and spectral analyses suggest substantial alignment of dominant token-space singular vectors. This is a plausible and interesting explanation for why cross-layer low-rank sharing can work where direct layer merging fails.

The proposed xKV method is conceptually simple and practically relevant: it performs post-training cross-layer SVD over grouped layer caches, requires no model retraining, and can be combined with selective reconstruction and quantization.

The empirical evaluation is fairly broad for this area, covering RULER, multi-turn NIAH, LongBench, several GQA models, and an appendix experiment on an MLA/MoE-style model. The main RULER results show that xKV preserves accuracy much better than single-layer SVD and MiniCache at much higher compression, and the SR variants compare favorably to ShadowKV at similar GPU-memory budgets.

The paper includes useful ablations on window size, key-only versus value-only compression, higher compression regimes, quantization compatibility, and memory/FLOP accounting. These strengthen the case that the gains are due to cross-layer factorization rather than only selective reconstruction.

The problem is significant: KV-cache memory and decode throughput are real bottlenecks for long-context LLM serving, and a plug-and-play method that can keep compressed keys and values on GPU would be valuable if reproduced.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is weaker than the claims require. The abstract says code is publicly available, but the extracted manuscript contains no visible URL. Several crucial implementation details are missing or under-specified, including exact ranks used in the main tables, randomized SVD parameters, numerical precision, custom kernel implementation details, token/chunk budgets beyond the 2k selection setting, outlier settings, and evaluation harness versions.

The strongest efficiency claims depend on a custom SVD kernel and system implementation, but the paper gives only a high-level description. The latency appendix has inconsistencies, e.g. text refers to A6000 while tables say A100, and the main efficiency evaluation is limited to a single A100 setting. Without released kernels or more detailed benchmarking methodology, the 4.23x throughput and negligible SVD-overhead claims are not fully verifiable.

Some presentation and consistency issues undermine confidence. The main text says the evaluated models include Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Qwen3-4B, while Table 1 reports Qwen2.5-14B; the abstract mentions DeepSeek-V2 among main models. Table 6 caption claims xKV achieves higher accuracy than full attention, but the shown averages are below full attention. These are not fatal, but they signal insufficient polishing.

The theoretical argument from high CKA to aligned dominant singular vectors is suggestive but not a guarantee strong enough to justify some wording. High CKA is a weighted aggregate over eigenspaces and does not by itself ensure that a single low-rank basis will preserve all task-relevant cache information, especially for rare tokens or adversarial long-context retrieval patterns.

The evaluation is convincing on RULER but less decisive elsewhere. On LongBench, xKV is competitive but not clearly better than SnapKV/PyramidKV in average accuracy, and gains over ShadowKV with SR are modest. There are no statistical error bars or repeated runs, and the benchmarks may not stress long generation, distribution shift, or very long outputs.

The limitations and ethics discussion are thin. The paper honestly notes that generated tokens are left uncompressed and long-generation scenarios are not addressed, which is an important limitation, but it does not discuss failure modes from approximate token selection, interactions with safety-critical retrieval, deployment energy/cost tradeoffs, or risks of using compressed caches in contexts requiring faithful recall.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: reducing KV-cache memory and latency for long-context LLM inference without retraining. The proposed cross-layer low-rank factorization is a plausible and useful direction, especially because it targets redundancy not exploited by standard per-layer compression.

The empirical evaluation covers several relevant baselines and benchmarks, including RULER, LongBench, multi-turn NIAH, token eviction, quantization, per-layer SVD, MiniCache, Quest, and ShadowKV. The reported accuracy numbers suggest that cross-layer factorization can preserve information better than naive per-layer SVD and inter-layer token merging.

The method is conceptually simple and potentially deployable: shared token bases per layer window plus layer-specific reconstruction matrices. The appendix also gives useful memory/FLOP accounting and ablations over window size, key/value compression, and quantization integration.
The limitations section honestly notes that the method mainly targets long-prefill settings and does not handle long-generation accumulation of newly generated KV states.
weaknesses: The central motivation is overstated. The manuscript repeatedly claims that high CKA implies aligned dominant singular vectors, but the provided derivation only shows a weighted aggregate overlap between Gram-matrix eigenvectors under centering. This does not by itself justify the stronger operational claim used for uncentered online SVD factorization of KV caches, nor does it establish that a single shared basis will be robust across prompts, layers, heads, and models.

The efficiency evidence is not yet convincing enough for the strongest claims. Dense xKV is reported to be slower than full attention in kernel latency, and the speedups rely on selective reconstruction borrowed from ShadowKV-style token selection. The paper does not sufficiently isolate how much of the end-to-end speedup comes from the new cross-layer factorization versus SR/offloading choices, batch-size changes, or avoiding OOM regimes.

Reproducibility is weak. The abstract says the code is publicly available but the URL is blank. Critical implementation details are missing or inconsistent: the main text says torch.svd_lowrank is used, while the appendix reports a custom randomized SVD kernel with 4x speedup; the hardware description for SVD overhead also appears inconsistent. Without code and kernel details, the latency and throughput claims are hard to verify.

The comparisons are sometimes confusing or potentially unfair. Compression ratios, total memory reduction, and effective GPU memory reduction are mixed across methods, especially for offloading-based baselines. xKV-SR is compared to ShadowKV variants under different total/GPU-memory regimes, and the paper does not provide enough sensitivity analysis over token budget, chunk size, outlier handling, rank allocation, or context length.

The experimental scope is narrower than the broad claims suggest. Most main results are at 64K context and on a small number of models; the DeepSeek/MLA and broader CKA studies are relegated to limited appendix plots. There is no variance reporting, no statistical uncertainty, and limited stress testing on long generation, diverse prompts, or production serving traces.

Presentation has several credibility-damaging issues: captions claim xKV achieves higher accuracy than full attention despite tables showing lower accuracy; model names and claims are inconsistent in places; some percentage improvements are reported ambiguously; and the impact statement is generic and does not discuss risks of enabling cheaper long-context inference or deployment tradeoffs.

strengths: The paper identifies a useful and non-obvious source of redundancy in long-context inference: even when token-wise cross-layer cosine similarity is low, CKA analysis suggests strong alignment among dominant left singular vectors of KV caches. This gives a convincing motivation for cross-layer factorization rather than simple layer merging.

The proposed xKV method is technically simple, plug-and-play, and practically relevant. It requires no retraining or architectural changes, compresses adjacent layers into a shared low-rank token basis with layer-specific reconstruction matrices, and extends naturally to selective reconstruction at decode time.

The empirical evidence is broad and mostly convincing. The paper evaluates RULER, multi-turn NIAH, LongBench, and code benchmarks, across Llama, Qwen, and DeepSeek/MLA-style architectures. Results show that xKV preserves accuracy at aggressive compression rates, often around 8x, and substantially outperforms single-layer SVD and MiniCache.

The efficiency study is valuable because it distinguishes dense reconstruction from selective reconstruction. The paper honestly shows dense xKV can be compute-bound, while xKV-SR yields meaningful throughput gains, including reported end-to-end speedups up to 4.23x on A100.

The appendices strengthen the submission with derivations connecting CKA to singular-vector alignment, selection algorithms, latency breakdowns, window-size ablations, key/value compression ablations, quantization compatibility, and broader CKA analysis.
weaknesses: Some reproducibility details are incomplete or inconsistent. The abstract says the code is publicly available but the URL appears blank; the main text says torch.svd_lowrank is used, while the appendix discusses a custom randomized SVD kernel; and the SVD overhead section mentions an A6000 in prose while tables report A100. These details matter for reproducing the latency claims.

The strongest systems claims would benefit from more detailed implementation disclosure: kernel details, memory accounting in actual bytes, batching/scheduling policy, prompt/output lengths, generated-token handling, and variance across runs are not fully specified.

The evaluation is strong but still centered on benchmarks with synthetic or structured long-context behavior. More real serving workloads, multi-request throughput experiments, and longer generation scenarios would better establish deployment significance.

The method inherits limitations from selective reconstruction/token selection. xKV-SR uses landmark-guided selection from ShadowKV, but the paper could more clearly separate the contribution of cross-layer factorization from the selection mechanism and analyze failure cases when selected chunks miss relevant tokens.

Several claims are phrased too strongly. For example, captions and discussion sometimes imply xKV outperforms full attention or all compression methods broadly, while the tables show small accuracy drops versus full attention and cases where token eviction baselines are competitive or slightly better.

The limitations and impact statement are thin. The paper notes that long generation is not addressed, but it does not deeply discuss verifier-free failure modes, approximation-induced hallucination or retrieval errors, or how compression behaves under adversarial or safety-critical long-context use.
